evidence.quote: As I walked to Geisenheimer's that night I was feeling blue and restless, tired of New York, tired of dancing, tired of everything.
evidence.paraphrase: The narrator expresses weariness and dissatisfaction with city life at the outset.

evidence.quote: There still come days in the spring when the country seems to get a stranglehold on me and start in pulling.
evidence.paraphrase: The narrator describes a recurring longing for the countryside.

evidence.quote: We weren't thinking on the same plane, Charlie and me. The way I had been feeling all day, what I wanted to talk about was last season's crops. The subject he fancied was this season's chorus-girls.
evidence.paraphrase: The narrator contrasts her rural yearning with Charlie's fascination with the city.

evidence.quote: If you're a professional dancer at Geisenheimer's, you aren't supposed to advertise the fact.
evidence.paraphrase: The narrator explains the hidden arrangement of paid professional dancers who secretly win the cup contest.

evidence.quote: I hate New York,' she said getting it out at last with a rush. 'I'm scared of it.
evidence.paraphrase: Mrs Charlie confesses her fear and hatred of the city.
Charlie reacts with fright at the suggestion his wife might leave him.

evidence.quote: He gave a kind of shiver. 'I never want to see it again in my life!' he said.
evidence.paraphrase: Charlie reverses his attitude and rejects the city entirely.

evidence.quote: That's what I think. I'm sick of this place, Izzy. I'm sick of dancing. I'm sick of New York. I'm sick of everything. I'm going back to the country.
evidence.paraphrase: The narrator decides to quit her job and change her life by returning to the country.

evidence.quote: She made you think of fresh milk and new-laid eggs and birds singing. To see her was like getting away to the country in August.
evidence.paraphrase: The narrator contrasts the rural wife's appeal against the city crowd's usual tastes.
